title: Macroeconomic objectives 1: low unemployment, low and stable rate of inflation

questions.prompt: Which of the following people in Veld would be counted as unemployed?

options.text: A 67-year-old who has retired and is not looking for work
options.misconception: Retired people above working age who are not seeking work are outside the labour force.

options.text: A 30-year-old who lost her job last month and is applying for new jobs
A 19-year-old full-time university student who is not looking for work
options.misconception: Students who are not seeking work are not in the labour force, so they are not unemployed.

options.text: A 45-year-old who stopped looking for work after a year of failed applications
options.misconception: This is a discouraged worker; because they are no longer seeking work, they are not counted as unemployed.

hints: Use the official conditions a person must meet to be counted as unemployed.
Check each person against age, whether they have a job, and whether they are actively searching.
questions.targets: Who counts as unemployed vs outside the labour force

questions.prompt: Define inflation.
marking_points: A sustained (continuing) increase [1]
in the general (average) price level of goods and services in an economy [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer includes both 'sustained' and 'general price level'; a rise in the price of one good is not enough.
hints: Think about what a price index such as the CPI measures over time.
Your answer should say how long the change lasts and which prices are involved.
questions.targets: Precise definition: sustained + general price level

questions.prompt: Define the unemployment rate.
marking_points: The number of unemployed people expressed as a percentage of the labour force [1]
where the unemployed are people of working age without a job who are actively seeking work [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the percentage relationship with the labour force (not the whole population) and describes who is unemployed.
hints: This is a rate, so it compares one group of people with a larger group.
State which two groups are compared and describe the people in the smaller group.
questions.targets: Unemployment rate uses the labour force, not the population

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of underemployment?

options.text: A worker who is between jobs for three weeks after moving city
options.misconception: This is frictional unemployment: the person has no job while searching.

options.text: A person who has given up looking for work
options.misconception: This is a discouraged worker, who is outside the labour force rather than employed.

options.text: A ski instructor who has no work during the summer
options.misconception: This is seasonal unemployment: the person has no job at that time of year.

options.text: A trained engineer working part-time as a delivery driver who wants full-time engineering work

hints: Underemployed people do have a job, so first remove anyone without work.
Then ask whose job uses fewer hours or lower skills than they want or have.
questions.targets: Underemployment vs types of unemployment

questions.prompt: A factory in Kuva replaces its assembly workers with robots. The workers' skills are no longer needed anywhere in the economy. What type of unemployment does this create?

options.text: Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
options.misconception: Frictional unemployment is short-term job search; here the workers' skills are no longer demanded at all.

options.text: Cyclical unemployment
options.misconception: Cyclical unemployment comes from a fall in AD in a downturn, not from a change in technology.

options.text: Seasonal unemployment
options.misconception: Seasonal unemployment follows the time of year; this job loss is permanent.

hints: Think about the cause of the job loss and how long it is likely to last.
Ask whether there is a mismatch between workers' skills and the jobs available.
questions.targets: Identifying structural unemployment from technological change

questions.prompt: Table 1 shows labour market data for Veld. Calculate the unemployment rate.

table.caption: Table 1: Veld's labour market
rows: Working age, not in the labour force

marking_points: Labour force = employed + unemployed = 36 + 4 = 40 million [1]
Unemployment rate = 4 / 40 × 100 = 10% [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Full marks for the correct labour force and a 10% unemployment rate with working; dividing by the working-age population (8%) earns 0 for the second mark.
hints: Not every row of Table 1 belongs in the calculation; decide which people make up the labour force.
Find the labour force first, then express the unemployed as a percentage of it.
questions.targets: Correct denominator: labour force, not working-age population

questions.prompt: Veld's consumer price index (CPI) is 120 in 2025, using 2020 as the base year. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Prices have risen by 120% since 2020
options.misconception: The base year has an index of 100, so the rise is measured from 100, not from zero.

options.text: The inflation rate in 2025 was 20%
options.misconception: The index compares 2025 with 2020, not with 2024, so it does not give one year's inflation rate.

options.text: On average, prices in 2025 are 20% higher than in 2020
Every good in the basket costs 20% more than in 2020
options.misconception: The CPI is an average; some prices may have risen more, less, or even fallen.

hints: Recall the value of a price index in its base year.
Compare the 2025 value with the base-year value, and think about what an average can and cannot tell you.
questions.targets: Interpreting an index number relative to the base year

questions.prompt: Table 2 shows Kuva's consumer price index. What was the rate of inflation between 2024 and 2025?

table.caption: Table 2: Kuva's consumer price index (base year 2020 = 100)

options.misconception: This is the change in index points, not the percentage change from 2024.
This compares 2025 with the base year value of 100, not with 2024.
This divides the change by the 2025 value instead of the earlier 2024 value.

hints: Use the percentage change formula with the two index values.
Find the change in the index, then divide by the value for the earlier year and multiply by 100.
questions.targets: Inflation rate from CPI: dividing by the earlier year

questions.prompt: Table 3 shows Tarsa's consumer price index. Calculate the rate of inflation between 2024 and 2025.

table.caption: Table 3: Tarsa's consumer price index (base year 2023 = 100)

marking_points: Inflation rate = 12.5% [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Correct working dividing by the 2024 value and an answer of 12.5% earns both marks.
hints: Pick the two index values for the years in the question; the base year value is not needed.
Apply the percentage change formula, dividing by the earlier year's value.
questions.targets: Inflation rate from a price index, not from the base year

questions.prompt: Table 4 shows Veld's annual inflation rate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Between 2022 and 2024 Veld experienced deflation
options.misconception: The inflation rate stayed positive, so the price level kept rising; only its speed fell.

options.text: The price level fell in 2024
options.misconception: A positive inflation rate of 2% means the price level still rose in 2024.

options.text: Between 2023 and 2024 Veld experienced disinflation
In 2025 Veld experienced disinflation
options.misconception: A negative inflation rate means the price level fell, which is deflation rather than disinflation.

hints: Look carefully at whether each inflation rate is positive or negative, and how it changes.
Separate a fall in the price level from a fall in the speed at which the price level is rising.
questions.targets: Disinflation vs deflation from data

questions.prompt: In Kuva, a worker's nominal wage rises by 3% over a year, while the inflation rate is 5%. What happens to the worker's purchasing power?

options.text: It rises by about 8%
options.misconception: This adds the two rates, but inflation reduces what a wage can buy rather than adding to it.

options.text: It rises by about 2%
options.misconception: This gets the size right but the direction wrong; prices rose faster than the wage.

options.text: It is unchanged because the wage has risen
options.misconception: A higher nominal wage does not protect purchasing power if prices rise even faster.

options.text: It falls by about 2%

hints: Purchasing power depends on the real value of the wage, not its nominal value.
Compare how fast the wage is growing with how fast prices are growing.
questions.targets: Real vs nominal wages and purchasing power

questions.prompt: Table 5 shows labour market data for Kuva. Which statement about the change from Year 1 to Year 2 is correct?

options.text: The unemployment rate fell to 6%
options.misconception: This divides by the Year 1 labour force; discouraged workers have left the labour force, so it is smaller in Year 2.

options.text: The unemployment rate fell to 6.25% even though no new jobs were created
The unemployment rate stayed at 10% because discouraged workers are still counted
options.misconception: Discouraged workers are not actively seeking work, so they are not counted as unemployed.

options.text: The unemployment rate rose because the labour force became smaller
options.misconception: A smaller labour force with fewer unemployed people gives a lower, not higher, rate here.

hints: Check which groups belong to the labour force in each year.
Work out the labour force for Year 2 first, then the rate, and compare the number employed in the two years.
questions.targets: Discouraged workers make the unemployment rate understate true unemployment

questions.prompt: Table 6 shows the typical household basket in Veld. Using 2024 as the base year, calculate the consumer price index (CPI) for 2025.
questions.model_answer_note: Both basket costs with working and a CPI of 114 earns full marks; own-figure rule applies for the last mark.
hints: Use the quantities in the basket together with the prices for each year.
Find the total cost of the same basket in each year, then express the later cost relative to the base-year cost.
questions.targets: Weighted basket cost and CPI calculation

questions.prompt: Distinguish between cyclical unemployment and structural unemployment.
marking_points: Cyclical unemployment is caused by a fall in aggregate demand during a downturn or recession [1]
Structural unemployment is caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available, e.g. due to technological change or changes in demand for industries [1]
Cyclical unemployment falls as the economy recovers, while structural unemployment is long-term and part of the natural rate [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the cause of each type and a clear difference in how long each lasts or how it is fixed.
hints: Use the business cycle for one type and changes in the structure of the economy for the other.
For each type, give its cause, then compare what happens to it when the economy grows again.
questions.targets: Cyclical vs structural unemployment

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely to cause cost-push inflation in Veld?

options.text: A rise in consumer confidence
options.misconception: Higher confidence raises consumption and AD, which causes demand-pull, not cost-push, inflation.

options.text: A cut in income tax
options.misconception: A tax cut raises disposable income and AD, which is a demand-pull cause.

options.text: Large nominal wage increases that are greater than productivity growth
A rise in labour productivity
options.misconception: Higher productivity lowers costs per unit of output, which reduces cost pressure.

hints: Cost-push inflation starts on the supply side of the AD-AS model.
Find the option that raises firms' costs per unit of output.
questions.targets: Cost-push from the labour market vs demand-pull causes

questions.prompt: Distinguish between demand-pull inflation and cost-push inflation.
marking_points: Demand-pull inflation is caused by an increase in aggregate demand (C, I, G or X − M) [1]
AD shifts right, so the price level rises and real GDP rises (towards or beyond potential) [1]
Cost-push inflation is caused by a rise in firms' costs of production, e.g. wages or imported raw materials [1]
SRAS shifts left, so the price level rises while real GDP falls [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives the cause of each type, the curve that shifts, and the different effect on real GDP.
hints: Use an AD-AS diagram for each type.
For each, name the cause, say which curve shifts and in which direction, then compare what happens to output.
questions.targets: Demand-pull vs cost-push on AD-AS

questions.prompt: Kuva signs a free trade agreement that removes tariffs on imported clothing. Explain how this could increase structural unemployment in Kuva.
marking_points: Cheaper imported clothing reduces demand for clothing made in Kuva [1]
Domestic clothing firms cut output or close, so workers lose their jobs [1]
These workers' skills do not match the jobs in growing industries (or they live in the wrong area), so unemployment is long-term / structural [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links trade to falling demand for a domestic industry, job losses, and a skills or location mismatch.
hints: Think about what happens to a domestic industry that now faces cheaper foreign competition.
Follow the chain from falling demand to job losses, then explain why these workers struggle to find other jobs.
questions.targets: Trade integration and structural unemployment

questions.prompt: The government of Veld sets a national minimum wage above the market equilibrium wage. Using a labour market diagram described in words, explain how this could cause unemployment.
marking_points: The minimum wage is a labour market rigidity set above the equilibrium wage (a price floor) [1]
At this wage the quantity of labour supplied rises and the quantity of labour demanded falls [1]
The excess supply of labour (the gap between the two quantities) is unemployment [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer describes the wage floor above equilibrium and identifies the excess supply of labour as unemployment.
hints: Use a labour market diagram with the wage rate on the vertical axis and demand and supply of labour.
Draw a line above the equilibrium wage and compare how many people want to work with how many workers firms want to hire.
questions.targets: Minimum wage and real-wage (structural) unemployment

questions.prompt: Explain two economic costs of high unemployment for Veld.
marking_points: Loss of real output: unemployed labour means the economy produces below its potential (inside its PPC) [1]
This output is lost for good, so incomes and living standards are lower than they could be [1]
Lower incomes reduce tax revenue for the government [1]
Spending on unemployment benefits rises, worsening the budget and leaving less for other uses [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Accept other valid costs (e.g. loss of skills/human capital, greater income inequality) where each is identified [1] and explained [1].
hints: Think about the effects on total output and on the government's budget.
For each cost, state it and then explain how it follows from people being out of work.
questions.targets: Economic costs of unemployment, including public finances

questions.prompt: Why might deflation harm the economy of Kuva?

options.text: Consumers delay purchases because they expect prices to fall further, so aggregate demand falls
It raises purchasing power, so it always increases consumer spending
options.misconception: Higher purchasing power can help, but expected further price falls give people a reason to wait before spending.

options.text: It makes Kuva's exports less competitive abroad
options.misconception: Falling domestic prices make exports cheaper, so this is not a cost of deflation.

options.text: It reduces the real value of debts that households owe
options.misconception: Deflation increases the real burden of debt, it does not reduce it.

hints: Think about how expectations of future prices affect spending decisions today.
Follow the chain from expected price changes to spending, to AD, to output and jobs.
questions.targets: Deferred consumption as a cost of deflation

questions.prompt: In Tarsa, inflation is unexpectedly 8% in a year, while banks pay and charge a fixed interest rate of 3%. Which group is most likely to gain?

options.text: Savers earning a fixed interest rate
options.misconception: Their interest is less than inflation, so the real value of their savings falls.

options.text: Pensioners on fixed nominal incomes
options.misconception: Their income buys less when prices rise, so they lose purchasing power.

options.text: Banks that have lent money at fixed rates
options.misconception: Lenders are repaid in money that is worth less, so they lose in real terms.

options.text: Borrowers with fixed-rate loans

hints: Compare the interest rate with the inflation rate to find the real interest rate.
Ask who is repaying money whose real value has fallen.
questions.targets: Redistributive effects of unexpected inflation

questions.prompt: Explain two limitations of using the consumer price index (CPI) to measure changes in the cost of living for households in Veld.
marking_points: Different households (e.g. pensioners, rural families) have spending patterns that differ from the typical basket [1]
So their actual rise in the cost of living may be higher or lower than the CPI shows [1]
Quality improvements and new products are not fully captured by the basket [1]
So part of a measured price rise may reflect better products, meaning the CPI can overstate inflation [1]
questions.model_answer_note: Accept other valid limitations (e.g. substitution towards cheaper goods, regional price differences, outdated weights) where each is identified [1] and explained [1].
hints: Think about how the basket and its weights are chosen and how often they change.
For each limitation, state it and then explain why it makes the CPI differ from a real household's experience.
questions.targets: Limitations of the CPI

questions.prompt: The zed, Veld's currency, depreciates sharply. Explain how this could cause both cost-push and demand-pull inflation in Veld.
marking_points: Imported raw materials and fuel become more expensive in zeds, raising firms' costs, so SRAS shifts left (cost-push) [1]
Veld's exports become cheaper for foreigners and imports dearer, so net exports rise [1]
AD shifts right, raising the price level (demand-pull) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer explains one supply-side channel through import costs and one demand-side channel through net exports.
hints: Think about how a depreciation changes the prices of imports and exports.
Trace one channel through firms' costs and another through a component of AD.
questions.targets: Depreciation as a cause of both types of inflation

questions.prompt: What does a short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) show?

options.text: A positive relationship between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate
options.misconception: A positive relationship would mean they rise together; the SRPC slopes downward.

options.text: An inverse relationship between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate
No relationship between inflation and unemployment at any time
options.misconception: That is closer to the long-run view; in the short run the curve shows a trade-off.

options.text: An inverse relationship between the inflation rate and real GDP
options.misconception: The Phillips curve plots inflation against unemployment, not against real GDP.

hints: Recall the two variables on the axes of the Phillips curve.
Think about which way the short-run curve slopes and what that says about the two variables.
questions.targets: What the SRPC shows

questions.prompt: Table 7 shows data for Veld. Which statement is best supported by the data?

options.text: From 2021 to 2023 the data are consistent with a movement along a single short-run Phillips curve
From 2023 to 2024 the data are consistent with a movement along a single short-run Phillips curve
options.misconception: Inflation and unemployment both rose, which cannot happen along a downward-sloping SRPC.

options.text: From 2021 to 2023 the data show the long-run Phillips curve shifting
options.misconception: A falling unemployment rate with rising inflation is a short-run trade-off, not evidence about the LRPC.

options.text: In 2024 Veld experienced disinflation
options.misconception: Inflation rose from 6% to 9%, so the rate of inflation increased.

hints: Look at the direction of change in both columns for each pair of years.
A movement along a downward-sloping curve means the two variables move in opposite directions.
questions.targets: Reading data for a trade-off vs a shift (stagflation)

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most likely move Kuva down along its existing short-run Phillips curve?

options.text: Expansionary monetary policy that raises aggregate demand
options.misconception: Higher AD lowers unemployment and raises inflation, which is a movement up the curve.

options.text: A large fall in world oil prices
options.misconception: A supply-side change shifts the SRPC rather than moving the economy along it.

options.text: Contractionary fiscal policy that reduces aggregate demand
Supply-side policies that lower the natural rate of unemployment
options.misconception: These shift the long-run Phillips curve to the left rather than moving along the SRPC.

hints: Movements along the SRPC come from changes in aggregate demand.
Decide which direction on the curve means lower inflation and higher unemployment, then find the policy that causes it.
questions.targets: Movement along vs shift of the SRPC

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the short-run Phillips curve and the long-run Phillips curve.
marking_points: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward, showing a trade-off between inflation and unemployment for a given expected inflation rate [1]
The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, showing no trade-off in the long run [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer states the shape and meaning of each curve.
hints: Use the shape of each curve on a diagram with inflation on the vertical axis.
For each curve, say what shape it has and what it implies about a trade-off.
questions.targets: SRPC vs LRPC

questions.prompt: Explain how a sharp rise in world oil prices could cause stagflation in Tarsa, with reference to the short-run Phillips curve.
marking_points: Higher oil prices raise firms' costs, so SRAS shifts left [1]
The price level rises while real GDP falls, so inflation and unemployment both increase [1]
This is shown by the short-run Phillips curve shifting to the right (outward) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links the supply shock to higher inflation and higher unemployment together and shows this as an outward SRPC shift.
hints: Start with an AD-AS diagram, then link it to a Phillips curve diagram.
Trace the cost change to the supply curve, then to both inflation and unemployment, then to the position of the SRPC.
questions.targets: Supply shock, stagflation and an SRPC shift

questions.prompt: According to the natural rate of unemployment hypothesis, the long-run Phillips curve is:

options.text: downward sloping, like the short-run curve
options.misconception: A downward slope would mean a lasting trade-off, which the hypothesis rejects.

options.text: horizontal at an inflation rate of zero
options.misconception: A horizontal curve would mean unemployment can change with no effect on inflation.

options.text: vertical at an unemployment rate of zero
options.misconception: Even in the long run there is frictional and structural unemployment, so the natural rate is above zero.

options.text: vertical at the natural rate of unemployment

hints: Link the long-run Phillips curve to the long-run aggregate supply curve.
Ask whether changes in inflation can change unemployment once expectations have adjusted.
questions.targets: Shape and position of the LRPC

questions.prompt: The government of Veld raises aggregate demand to push unemployment below its natural rate. Explain, using the natural rate of unemployment hypothesis, what will happen in the long run.
marking_points: In the short run, higher AD raises inflation and lowers unemployment: a movement up along the SRPC [1]
Workers come to expect higher inflation and demand higher nominal wages [1]
Firms' costs rise, SRAS shifts left and the SRPC shifts right, so unemployment returns to the natural rate [1]
The long-run result is higher inflation with no lasting fall in unemployment, shown by a vertical LRPC [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer covers the short-run movement, the role of inflation expectations and wages, and the long-run return to the natural rate at higher inflation.
hints: Use a diagram with a short-run and a long-run Phillips curve.
Trace the steps: the short-run effect, then how expectations and wages adjust, then where the economy ends up.
questions.targets: Long-run Phillips curve and expectations
